lead: GNSS finds a receiver position from the travel times of radio signals from several satellites whose positions are known. GPS is the United States system; GNSS is the family that also includes GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC. A surveyor uses GNSS for control points, stake-out, machine guidance and monitoring. The receiver measures a range to each satellite, reads the satellite position from the navigation message, and solves for latitude, longitude, height and its own clock error. One setup can give centimetre positions when two receivers share carrier-phase observations.
prereq: You need: datums and coordinate systems from Unit 1, control surveys from Unit 4, and the total station from 5.1 for comparison.

blocks.text: The space segment is the satellite constellation. Each satellite carries atomic clocks, radios and a processor. It broadcasts a navigation message that contains its broadcast ephemeris: the orbital parameters a receiver uses to compute the satellite position at the signal transmission time. The control segment tracks every satellite from monitor stations, computes orbit and clock corrections at a master control station, and uploads them. The user segment is the receiver and its antenna.

Each signal has three parts. The carrier is the radio wave, such as L1 or L5. The code is a known binary pattern that lets the receiver align its copy with the incoming signal. The navigation message carries orbit, clock and health data. Code alignment gives a pseudorange: a range that is biased by clock errors. Carrier phase counts cycles, precise to millimetres, but starts with an unknown whole number of cycles, called the ambiguity.

blocks.where: ρ is the measured pseudorange in metres; c = 299,792,458 m/s; t<sub>r</sub> is the true reception time in system (GPS) time in seconds, equal to the receiver clock reading minus δt<sub>r</sub>; t<sub>s</sub> is the satellite transmission time in system time in seconds; δt<sub>r</sub> is the receiver clock bias in seconds, positive when the receiver clock is ahead. In words, measured pseudorange = true range + c δt<sub>r</sub> = c(t<sub>r</sub> − t<sub>s</sub>) + c δt<sub>r</sub>, so a receiver clock that is ahead makes every pseudorange too long, and the bias is subtracted when correcting.

blocks.text: Four satellites give four pseudoranges. The unknowns are receiver x, y, z and δtr. Three satellites give three equations for four unknowns, so the receiver cannot solve. Satellite spread in the sky then decides how range error becomes position error; see 5.3.

Absolute positioning uses one receiver. Single-point positioning (SPP) uses code pseudoranges and broadcast ephemeris. Accuracy is a few metres. Relative positioning uses two or more receivers. The base sits on a known point; the rover works nearby. Differencing cancels common errors: satellite clock, most ionosphere and troposphere delay, and orbit error.

DGPS corrects code ranges. The base compares measured and known ranges and sends corrections; the rover applies them. This gives metre-level results. RTK uses carrier phase. The base and rover track the same satellites; the baseline is solved to centimetre level once the integer ambiguities are fixed. Network RTK uses a network of permanent stations, called CORS, to model corrections over an area; the rover receives a service message.

Survey modes: static, fast static and kinematic. Static keeps receivers still for long sessions for long baselines and high accuracy. Fast static shortens the occupation with dual-frequency data. Kinematic moves the rover, with ambiguity fixed at the start. Code is robust and instant; phase is precise but needs ambiguity resolution.

A receiver has an antenna, a radio-frequency front end, channels, a processor and storage. Channels track several satellites at once. Accuracy classes run from hand-held metre, to mapping sub-metre, to survey centimetre with RTK. GPS is one GNSS; a multi-constellation receiver tracks GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC. More satellites help in cities and under trees, but geometry still matters.

GPS coordinates are expressed in WGS84, a global geocentric datum. Receivers from other constellations transform their positions into WGS84, so GNSS output is normally in WGS84. Survey work often uses a local datum and a map projection. UTM is a common working frame: zones, easting, northing, metres. A datum transformation converts WGS84 coordinates to the local grid. Projection mathematics is in Unit 1 and Unit 7; do not repeat it here.

Errors. Satellite clock and ephemeris errors come from the broadcast data. Ionosphere delay varies with electron content; dual-frequency data remove most of it. Troposphere delay depends on pressure, temperature and humidity; models reduce it. Multipath is signal arrival after reflection from buildings or ground. Receiver noise is internal. Corrections come from differencing, models, dual frequency, choke-ring antennas and good site selection.

Other constellations: GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (Europe), BeiDou (China), NavIC (India). GPS modernization adds new civil signals such as L2C, L5 and L1C and new satellites. Multi-frequency, multi-constellation receivers are now normal.

figure.caption: GNSS positioning splits into absolute single-receiver SPP and relative methods. DGPS corrects code to metre level; RTK uses carrier phase to centimetre level, with Network RTK getting a service from CORS.

spec.aria: Tree of GNSS positioning methods: absolute single-receiver SPP, and relative methods DGPS and RTK, with Network RTK using CORS.

examples.question: A GNSS receiver clock is ahead by 10 µs. It measures pseudoranges 20,200,000.000 m, 21,000,000.000 m, 19,800,000.000 m and 22,500,000.000 m. Take c = 299,792,458 m/s. Find the common range error and the corrected pseudoranges.
steps: Convert the clock bias: 10 µs = 10 × 10⁻⁶ s = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ s.
A receiver clock ahead makes each measured pseudorange too long by this amount. Corrected range = measured − error.
examples.answer: The common range error is about 2997.925 m; corrected pseudoranges are 20,197,002.075 m, 20,997,002.075 m, 19,797,002.075 m and 22,497,002.075 m.

traps: Three satellites are not enough. The receiver clock bias is a fourth unknown; four satellites give four equations.
A receiver clock ahead gives pseudoranges that are too long; subtract the common error. Do not add it.
Code pseudorange is metre-level and instant; carrier phase is millimetre-level but has an integer ambiguity.
WGS84 and UTM are not the same: WGS84 is a datum; UTM is a projected grid in metres.
Convert µs to s before multiplying by c; 1 µs = 10⁻⁶ s.

quiz.a: Space segment (satellites), control segment (master control and monitor stations), and user segment (receivers and antennas).

quiz.q: Why does a receiver need the broadcast ephemeris?
quiz.a: The broadcast ephemeris gives the satellite orbital parameters and clock data. The receiver uses it to compute each satellite position at signal transmission time, which is needed in the range equations.

quiz.q: A receiver clock is 2 µs fast. One measured pseudorange is 20,000,000.000 m. Take c = 299,792,458 m/s. Find the corrected pseudorange.
Why does DGPS improve accuracy over single-point positioning?
quiz.a: The base receiver sits on a known point and measures the same satellite signals as the rover. Common errors such as satellite clock, orbit and much of the atmospheric delay are nearly the same at both ends. Differencing or applying the base correction removes most of them.

quiz.q: State one difference between code pseudorange and carrier-phase observation.
quiz.a: Code pseudorange is an unambiguous but noisy range, usually metre-level. Carrier phase is very precise but includes an unknown integer number of cycles, so ambiguity resolution is needed.

quiz.q: Why can a multi-constellation receiver help in an urban survey?
quiz.a: It can track more satellites from GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC. More satellites improve availability when buildings block part of the sky, but position quality still depends on satellite geometry and DOP.

quiz.q: Name two satellite navigation systems other than GPS.
quiz.a: Any two of GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC.

beyond: Not for the exam. Precise point positioning uses precise satellite orbits and clocks with dual-frequency phase data, without a nearby base station. CORS networks now support many surveying and machine-control tasks over wide areas. Dual-frequency smartphones are making metre-level positioning common in daily apps. Search for PPP, CORS and multi-frequency GNSS to go further.
